data.title: review the constitutional legislative lists .
data.promise_blog:
Promise Title: Review the Constitutional legislative lists to ensure that States are given greater control over certain critical matters. Focus areas will include, crime prevention, prisons, stamp duties and certain forms of taxation.

Nigeria’s 1999 Constitution, crafted during military rule, centralises power in a way that often clashes with the realities of governing a diverse, decentralised nation. The Exclusive Legislative List which reserves 68 key areas, including policing, prisons, and taxation, for the federal government—has long stifled subnational innovation. Calls to revise this list, particularly granting states greater control over crime prevention, prisons, stamp duties, and select taxes, are not just bureaucratic tinkering. They represent a critical step toward addressing Nigeria’s most persistent crises: insecurity, economic stagnation, and systemic inequity.

The need for greater resources control has been emphasised over the years as it is one of the pillars of federalism; Nigeria since gaining independence has seen many decisions made from Abuja, most of which are not peculiar to the local settings of respective states, thereby creating frictions.

This promise focused on review of constitutional lists to enable states to take responsibility and take care of these important items. This promise will be tracked by the government efforts in ensuring the removal of legislative restrictions on states to assume these items.

updates.blog:
RESHAPING FEDERALISM: PROGRESS ON POLICING, TAX, AND POWER REFORMS UNDER THE CURRENT ADMINISTRATION

The President has taken deliberate steps to devolve more powers to the states by liberalising items on the exclusive legislative list, A major development came in 2023 when the National Assembly established a Constitution Review Committee to examine the legal framework for state police.

In the area of taxation, the administration achieved another milestone with the passage of a new tax bill, signed into law by the President. This legislation not only broadens the scope of taxes that states can collect but also repeals the obsolete stamp tax law, replacing it with a simplified version that boosts state revenues.

Together, these reforms underscore the President’s commitment to decentralisation, strengthening state autonomy, and advancing fiscal federalism through improved taxation rights and localised policing structures. This promise is currently rated in the works.
